mainTopic: The oaths a woman takes to collect her כתובה: Torah or rabbinic, and when they apply
overview: The amud opens with the end of the משנה. רבי שמעון says the heirs can make the widow swear only when she is claiming her כתובה. The גמרא then asks what kind of oath a פוגמת takes, meaning a woman who admits part of her כתובה was already paid. רמי בר חמא suggests it is the Torah's oath of מודה במקצת. רבא rejects this and says it is a rabbinic oath, meant to make her remember exactly what she received. The גמרא then asks three questions about this oath. Does she swear if the partial payment had witnesses? A proof is brought and pushed off. Does listing tiny payments make her believable? That one ends in תיקו. Does a פוחתת, who says the total is smaller but that she received nothing, swear? A ברייתא says she collects without an oath, as long as she claims a private trust agreement. Finally, רמי בר חמא suggests that the oath against one witness who says the כתובה was paid is a Torah oath. רבא again rejects this and calls it a rabbinic oath, meant to put the husband's mind at ease. The amud ends as רב פפא begins a statement that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: Heirs make her swear only if she claims her כתובה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends with רבי שמעון's rule: the heirs can make the widow take an oath only while she is claiming her כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: Whenever she claims her כתובה, the heirs make her swear. If she does not claim her כתובה, the heirs do not make her swear.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the משנה. רבי שמעון says the heirs' power to make the woman swear depends on whether she is asking to collect her כתובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heirs can demand an oath only as the price for paying her. If she is not asking them for her כתובה money, they have no grounds to make her swear.

keyTerms.meaning: She claims or demands payment
Her כתובה, the money promised to her in the marriage contract
Heirs (here, the husband's heirs)
Make someone take an oath

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
Whenever she claims her marriage contract payment,
the heirs make her take an oath.
And if she does not claim her marriage contract payment,
the heirs do not make her take an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the משנה, which began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Heirs may make the widow swear only when she claims her כתובה.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: Her oath is the Torah's oath for a partial admission
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא suggests that a woman who admits part of her כתובה was paid swears a Torah oath, because she is admitting part of a claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא thought it was a Torah oath. The husband claims he paid two hundred, and she admits one hundred. That is admitting part of a claim, and anyone who admits part of a claim must swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by asking where the woman's oath comes from. רמי בר חמא proposes that it is the Torah's oath of מודה במקצת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He compares her to a defendant who admits part of what is claimed against him. The husband claims she was fully paid, and she admits only partial payment. So she seems to fit the Torah rule that a partial admitter must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say (an idea that may later be rejected)
An oath required by the Torah
One who admits part of the claim
Claims

steps.confusionAlert: Usually the one admitting part of a claim is a defendant who owes money. Here the 'admitter' is the woman, and the husband's side is claiming that she was already paid.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rami bar Chama thought to say
that it is an oath from the Torah,
phrases.notes: He means the oath of the woman in the משנה who admits that part of her כתובה was already paid.

phrases.english: since he claims he paid two hundred
and she admits to him one hundred.
That is an admission to part of the claim,
and anyone who admits to part of a claim
must take an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by explaining the source of the oath discussed in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposal: her oath is the Torah oath of מודה במקצת.

steps.title: רבא gives two reasons it cannot be a Torah oath
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's idea. Torah oaths free a person from paying, but she swears in order to collect. Also, there is no Torah oath on claims involving liens on land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: There are two answers to this. First, everyone who swears in the Torah swears and does not pay, but she swears and collects. Second, there is no oath on a denial of a lien on land.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא knocks down the suggestion that this is a Torah oath. He gives two separate reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, a Torah oath is always taken by someone who wants to avoid paying, while this woman swears so that she can take money. Second, the Torah oaths do not apply to claims tied to land, and a כתובה is backed by a lien on the husband's land.

keyTerms.meaning: Two refutations of this idea
They swear and do not pay
She swears and collects
A lien on land
Denial of a claim

phrases.english: Rava said:
There are two answers against this.
One: everyone who takes an oath in the Torah
swears and does not pay,
but she swears and collects.

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹד: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל כְּפִירַת שִׁעְבּוּד קַרְקָעוֹת.
phrases.english: And furthermore: one does not swear over a denial of a lien on land.
phrases.notes: A כתובה is backed by the husband's land, so this rule applies to her claim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רמי בר חמא's proposal from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that her oath is a Torah oath of מודה במקצת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Torah oaths free the swearer from paying, while she swears to collect; Torah oaths also do not apply to liens on land.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The case does not match the Torah oath in direction (collecting instead of avoiding payment) or in subject (a claim backed by land).

steps.title: רבא: It is a rabbinic oath that makes her remember carefully
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the oath is rabbinic. The person who pays remembers exactly, but the person who receives money does not, so the חכמים required her to swear so that she would think carefully.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: It is a rabbinic oath. The one who pays remembers exactly, and the one who gets paid does not. So the חכמים put an oath on her so that she will be exact.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the Torah explanation, רבא gives the real reason for the oath: it is a rabbinic enactment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who pays out money pays close attention, but a person who receives money may not track it carefully. The oath pushes her to think hard about how much she actually received before she collects the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces a replacement explanation)
From rabbinic law
Is precise or careful
The one who is paid
They placed or imposed

steps.whatToRemember: The oath of a woman who admits partial payment of her כתובה is rabbinic, not a Torah oath. Its purpose is to make her remember exactly how much she received.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because the oath is rabbinic, it rests on a practical concern about memory, not on the Torah rules of מודה במקצת.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It is a rabbinic oath.
The one who pays is precise,
but the one who is paid is not precise.
So the Rabbis placed an oath on her
so that she will be precise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected Torah-oath explanation with a rabbinic one.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Her oath is rabbinic, so that the woman who received money will be careful about how much she received.

steps.title: Does she swear if the partial payment was made in front of witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a פוגמת כתובתה still has to swear when the part she admits receiving was paid in front of עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: a woman admits she was paid part of her כתובה, and that part was paid in front of witnesses. What is the law? We could say that if he had really paid her the rest, he would have used witnesses for that too, so she doesn't need to swear. Or maybe he just happened to have witnesses around that one time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. We already learned that a woman who admits partial payment must swear (a rabbinic oath). Now it asks whether this changes when the partial payment had witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side: the husband's habit was to pay with witnesses. Since nobody saw him pay the rest, he probably never paid it, so she should not need an oath. Other side: witnesses being present once may have been chance, and he could have paid the rest privately, so she still swears.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the Sages (an open question)
A woman who 'dents' her כתובה by admitting part of it was already paid
In front of witnesses
It just happened that way, by chance

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
A woman who admits part of her כתובה was paid, in front of witnesses, what is the law?
phrases.notes: She says part was paid, and witnesses saw that part being paid.

phrases.english: If it were true that he paid her the rest,
he would have paid her with witnesses,
or perhaps he just happened to have witnesses that time?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבא's rabbinic oath for a פוגמת and asks whether witnesses to the partial payment remove it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a woman who admits a partial payment made before witnesses must still swear to collect the rest.

steps.title: Attempted proof from the list of people who swear and collect
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה listing people who swear and collect, including 'one who reduces his document without witnesses,' and infers that with witnesses there is no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: everyone who swears a Torah oath swears and does not pay. But these people swear and collect: a hired worker, someone who was robbed, someone who was injured, someone whose opponent can't be trusted with an oath, a storekeeper relying on his account book, and someone who admits part of his loan document was paid without witnesses. So without witnesses he swears, but with witnesses he does not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from a משנה. Because the משנה says 'without witnesses,' it seems that with witnesses there is no oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depends on reading the words 'שלא בעדים' as an exact limit. If the oath applies only when there were no witnesses, then a partial payment with witnesses would need no oath, and she would collect the rest freely.

keyTerms.meaning: They swear and collect (the oath lets them take money)
Suspected of swearing falsely
A storekeeper's account book
One who admits part of his loan document was already paid

phrases.english: Come and hear:
All who swear an oath of the Torah
swear and do not pay.
And these swear and collect:
the hired worker, the one who was robbed, the one who was injured,
and one whose opponent is suspected regarding oaths,
and a storekeeper on his account book,
and one who admits part of his document was paid, without witnesses.
Without witnesses, yes; with witnesses, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer the question of step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That a partial payment made with witnesses needs no oath for the rest.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in שבועות that lists 'הפוגם שטרו שלא בעדים' among those who swear and collect.

steps.title: The proof is rejected: the משנה means 'it goes without saying'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the משנה speaks in a 'לא מיבעיא' style: with witnesses she surely swears; the new point is that she swears even without witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is speaking in a 'no need to say' style. There is no need to say that with witnesses she certainly needs an oath. But without witnesses, I might have said she is like someone who returns a lost object and can collect without an oath. So the משנה teaches us that she swears even then.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the proof. The words 'without witnesses' are not a limit; they describe the harder case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without witnesses, nobody could prove any payment, so her admitting part looks very honest, like returning a lost object. That might have freed her from an oath. The משנה teaches that she swears even there, and with witnesses she swears all the more, so the original question cannot be answered from here.

keyTerms.meaning: It is speaking in an 'it goes without saying' style
One who returns a lost object (trusted without an oath)
It teaches us (the new point)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying that with witnesses she is free from the oath. It says the opposite: with witnesses she surely swears. The משנה just mentions the less obvious case.

phrases.english: It is speaking in a 'no need to say' style:
There is no need to say that with witnesses
she certainly needs an oath,
but without witnesses,
I might say she should be like one who returns a lost object
phrases.notes: Without witnesses, he couldn't prove any payment, so her admitting part is like handing back something he had lost.

phrases.english: and she should take the money without an oath,
so it teaches us that she still swears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn from the משנה in step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof; the question of step 5 is not answered either way.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'שלא בעדים' was a limit, but it is really the harder, less obvious case.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה in שבועות does not prove anything about payment with witnesses. It only teaches that even without witnesses the woman swears and is not treated like one who returns a lost object.

steps.title: Does listing tiny payments make her trustworthy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a woman who carefully lists payments of less than a פרוטה each is believed without an oath, or whether this may be a trick.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: a woman reduces her כתובה by listing tiny amounts, each less than a פרוטה. What is the law? Do we say that since she is so careful, she must be telling the truth? Or maybe she is being clever to fool us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second, separate question about the same oath. Can great exactness about tiny sums replace the oath?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the oath exists so she will think carefully. Here she has already shown extreme carefulness, so maybe the oath's purpose is already met. On the other hand, the detailed list could be a trick to look honest.

keyTerms.meaning: Less than the value of a פרוטה, the smallest coin that counts
She is exact and careful
The truth
She is acting slyly or deceiving

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
A woman who admits part of her כתובה was paid
by small amounts, each less than a פרוטה, what is the law?
Do we say:
since she is so precise,
she is telling the truth,
or perhaps she is being sly?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: הַפּוֹגֶמֶת כְּתוּבָּתָהּ פָּחוֹת פָּחוֹת מִשָּׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question about the same oath of a פוגמת, unrelated to the witnesses question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether great precision about tiny payments frees her from the oath.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the question with תיקו: no answer is found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot answer the question about tiny payments, so it leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides are reasonable: her precision may show honesty, or it may be a trick. No source decides between them.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Both questions here end without a firm answer. The witnesses question had its proof rejected, and the tiny-payments question ends with תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of step 8 without a resolution.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether listing payments of less than a פרוטה frees her from the oath remains undecided.

steps.title: Does a woman who lowers her כתובה amount have to swear?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a פוחתת is treated like a פוגמת and must swear, or whether she is different because she does not admit to receiving anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: What is the law for a woman who lowers the amount of her כתובה? Is she the same as a פוגמת, or is she different? A פוגמת admits to part of the claim, but this woman admits to nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question about a woman who says her כתובה is worth less than what is written, but says she received nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פוגמת says she already got part of the money, so she partly agrees with the husband. That is why she must swear. A פוחתת does not agree that she got anything. She only says the total was smaller, so maybe she does not need an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked of them; an open question
A woman who lowers the amount of her כתובה
Admits to part of the claim
Or perhaps; introduces the other side of a question

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up פוגמת and פוחתת. A פוגמת says 'I got part of it already.' A פוחתת says 'I got nothing, but the total was smaller.'

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
A woman who reduces her כתובה, what is the law?
phrases.notes: She says the real amount is smaller than what is written, but she still says she was paid nothing.

phrases.english: Do we say this is the same as one who vitiates it,
or perhaps: one who vitiates admits to part of the claim,
but this one does not admit to part of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question that follows from the earlier discussion of פוגמת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a פוחתת must swear like a פוגמת, or collects without an oath because she does not admit to partial payment.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the woman who lowers her amount collects without an oath
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a פוחתת collects without an oath. It gives the example of a 1000 זוז כתובה where she says it is only a מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A woman who lowers her כתובה collects without an oath. How so? Her כתובה said a thousand זוז. Her husband said, 'You were already paid.' She said, 'I was not paid, and it is only a מנה.' She collects without an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that answers the question: the פוחתת collects without swearing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats the פוחתת differently from the פוגמת. Since she does not admit to receiving any money, she is not 'admitting to part,' so the oath of the פוגמת does not apply to her. This answers the second side of the question in step 10.

keyTerms.meaning: Without an oath
A מנה, which equals one hundred זוז
How so? Introduces an example

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who reduces her כתובה collects without an oath.
How so?
Her כתובה was a thousand זוז,
and he said to her, "You have received your כתובה,"
and she says, "I have not received it,
and it is only a מנה"
phrases.notes: A מנה is one hundred זוז, so she is claiming only a tenth of what is written.

phrases.english: she collects without an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פּוֹחֶתֶת תִּפָּרַע שֶׁלֹּא בִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to answer the question in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That a פוחתת collects without an oath.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that explicitly rules that a פוחתת collects without an oath.

steps.title: How can she collect with a document she says is false?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how she can collect at all. She herself says the document's 1000 זוז is wrong, so the document should be worthless.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what does she collect? With this document? This document is just a broken piece of clay!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. If she says the written amount is untrue, she seems to be calling her own document false.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A document that its owner admits is false has no value. So it is unclear how she can collect even the מנה using it.

keyTerms.meaning: With what does she collect?
A legal document
Just a broken piece of clay; worthless

phrases.english: With what does she collect?
With this document?
This document is merely a piece of clay!
phrases.notes: Since she says the 1000 written in it is wrong, she is calling her own document false.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא brought in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a פוחתת collects.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By her own claim the document records a false sum, so it is invalid and she has nothing to collect with.

steps.title: She claims there was a private trust agreement
steps.stepSummary: רבא בריה דרבה explains that she says the large sum was written on purpose, with a private understanding that she would only claim part of it. So the document itself is real.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא, son of רבה, said: The ברייתא is talking about a woman who says, 'There was a trust agreement between me and him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by describing the woman's claim more exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She does not say the document is fake. She says the two of them agreed privately that the big number was written but she would only collect a מנה. So the document is valid, and she can collect the smaller amount with it.

keyTerms.meaning: A trust agreement; a private understanding
Between me and him

steps.whatToRemember: A פוחתת collects without an oath, as long as she explains the larger written sum as a private trust agreement. Then the document stays valid.

phrases.english: רבא son of רבה said:
It is where she says, "There was a trust agreement between me and him."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה: בְּאוֹמֶרֶת אֲמָנָה הָיְתָה לִי בֵּינִי לְבֵינוֹ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the ברייתא is about a specific kind of claim.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: She is saying the document is false, so it should be worthless.
steps.terutzMaskana: She says the document is real and the extra amount was written by private agreement, so she can collect the smaller amount with it.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא suggests the one-witness oath is from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of one witness who says the כתובה was paid. רמי בר חמא suggests the oath there is a Torah oath, and supports it from a פסוק and a general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One witness testifies that it was paid.' רמי בר חמא thought this is a Torah oath. The פסוק says, 'One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity or for any sin.' That means one witness cannot be used for punishments, but he can obligate an oath. And the Master said: Wherever two witnesses would make him pay money, one witness makes him swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the משנה's one-witness case, and רמי בר חמא suggests what kind of oath it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק limits one witness only for 'iniquity and sin,' so we learn that one witness does count for an oath. Two witnesses saying she was paid would cancel her money claim, so one witness should obligate her to swear from the Torah. The words 'סבר למימר' hint that this idea may be questioned next.

keyTerms.meaning: One witness
Paid; the כתובה was already paid
An oath required by the Torah
He thought to say; a first suggestion

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether the oath is from the Torah or from the חכמים affects its rules, so this sets up the coming discussion.

phrases.english: "One witness testifies that it was paid."
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting our משנה here to start talking about it.

phrases.english: רמי בר חמא thought to say
that it is an oath by Torah law,
as it is written:
"One witness shall not rise up against a man
for any iniquity or for any sin."

phrases.aramaic: לְכׇל עָוֹן וּלְכׇל חַטָּאת הוּא דְּאֵינוֹ קָם,
phrases.english: It is for any iniquity or any sin that he does not rise up,
but he does rise up for an oath.
And the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁהַשְּׁנַיִם מְחַיְּיבִין אוֹתוֹ מָמוֹן —
phrases.english: Any place where two witnesses obligate him to pay money,
one witness obligates him to take an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֵד אֶחָד מְעִידָהּ שֶׁהִיא פְּרוּעָה. סְבַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא לְמֵימַר שְׁבוּעָה דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the פוחתת discussion and turns to another case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רמי בר חמא's first suggestion, the oath required when one witness says the כתובה was paid is a Torah oath, based on the rule that one witness obligates an oath wherever two would obligate money.

steps.title: רבא gives two reasons the oath cannot be from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's claim that the wife's oath is a Torah oath. Torah oaths free a person from paying, but she swears in order to collect. Also, there is no Torah oath on a denied lien on land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: There are two answers against this. First, everyone who swears in the Torah swears so that he does not have to pay, but she swears in order to take. Second, we do not swear about a denial of a lien on land.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רמי בר חמא from the previous step, who said the wife's oath is a Torah oath. He gives two separate reasons why that cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is about how Torah oaths work: they protect the one being sued from paying, but here the wife swears so she can collect money. The second reason is about what is being claimed: a כתובה is a lien on the husband's land, and the Torah never requires an oath over land claims.

keyTerms.meaning: Two answers, meaning two arguments against a claim
They swear and do not pay. A Torah oath frees the one who swears from paying.
She swears and takes. Her oath gets her money instead of freeing her from paying.
Denial of a claim
A lien on land, meaning someone's land is held as backing for a debt

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבא is saying the wife swears for no reason. He only argues that her oath cannot be a Torah oath. In the next step he explains where it does come from.

phrases.english: Rava said:
There are two answers in the matter.
phrases.notes: He means two arguments against רמי בר חמא's idea that this is a Torah oath.

phrases.english: One: that all who swear in the Torah
swear and do not pay,
but she swears and takes.
And furthermore: one does not swear
over a denial of a lien on land.
phrases.notes: A כתובה is backed by the husband's land, so this claim counts as a claim about land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רמי בר חמא's suggestion from step 14 that the oath is a Torah oath.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects the idea that the wife's oath against one witness is a Torah oath.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Torah oaths free the defendant from paying instead of letting a claimant collect, and the Torah gives no oath over liens on land.

steps.title: רבא says the oath is rabbinic, to reassure the husband
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the wife's oath is מדרבנן. The חכמים required it so the husband would feel at ease that he is not paying for nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The oath is rabbinic, to put the husband's mind at ease.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the Torah-oath idea has been rejected, רבא gives his own answer: the oath is a rabbinic rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is one witness saying the כתובה was already paid, so the husband has reason to feel he is being treated unfairly. The חכמים added an oath so he can feel sure the wife is telling the truth before he pays.

keyTerms.meaning: From the Rabbis, meaning a rabbinic rule and not a Torah rule
To put his mind at ease, to calm him
Husband

steps.whatToRemember: The oath of a wife facing one witness who says she was paid is not a Torah oath. It is a rabbinic oath, made to put the husband's mind at ease.
steps.whyThisMatters: Whether an oath is from the Torah or from the חכמים can change how strictly it is applied. This sets up the discussion that follows.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It is rabbinic,
in order to put the husband's mind at ease.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected Torah-oath explanation with a rabbinic one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife's oath against one witness who says she was paid is a rabbinic oath, meant to reassure the husband.
